_comment: Frequency band database for France. Edit bands, calibration, and logging freely.

calibration._comment_offset: Adjust to calibrate dBFS → dBm. E.g. set -30 if your setup typically reads ~30 dB above actual. Requires a known reference signal or calibrated source.

logging._comment_dedup_hz: Frequency resolution for deduplication — signals within this window count as the same source.

bands.name: Longwave (LW) Broadcast
bands.notes: French and European LW broadcast stations. Normal signal.

bands.name: NFC / HF RFID (13.56 MHz)
bands.notes: ISM band at 13.56 MHz. Signals normally very short-range (<10 cm for NFC). A visible signal here usually means a reader is nearby.

bands.name: Mediumwave (AM) Broadcast
bands.notes: Normal AM broadcast. HackRF has limited sensitivity here.

bands.name: Switching PSU / LED Driver RFI (HF)
likely_sources: CPL / Powerline adapter (courants porteurs en ligne)
bands.notes: Broadband HF RFI typical of switch-mode electronics. Look for harmonics spaced at the switching frequency (typically 25–200 kHz apart). Onduleurs solaires are a very common source in France.

bands.name: Amateur 6m Band / Low VHF RFI
bands.notes: Signals here from domestic electronics are likely RFI harmonics.

bands.name: VHF RFI / Switching PSU Harmonics
bands.notes: Any broadband or harmonic signal here not matching a known service is likely a domestic RFI source. HDMI and PSU harmonics are very common.

bands.name: FM Broadcast (87.5–108 MHz)
likely_sources: France Inter (87.8, 91.7, 94.0, 95.9, 99.0 MHz — varies by city)
NRJ, RTL, Europe 1, BFM Radio, RFM, Chérie FM, etc.
bands.notes: Normal FM broadcast. RDS subcarrier at ±57 kHz. Unusually strong local FM may indicate a pirate transmitter.

bands.name: VHF Aviation (108–118 MHz) — VOR / ILS / Nav
VHF Aviation Voice (118–137 MHz)
bands.notes: AM modulated, 25 kHz or 8.33 kHz channel spacing in Europe.

bands.name: DAB/DAB+ Digital Radio (174–230 MHz)
likely_sources: DAB multiplexes (France Bleu, Radio France, NRJ, RTL, BFM, etc.)
Block 5A-12D, various channel widths of 1.536 MHz
bands.notes: DAB is being deployed in France but coverage is still limited outside major cities.

bands.name: TETRA Emergency Services — Acropol/INPT (380–400 MHz)
bands.notes: French public safety TETRA network. Encrypted — decoding is illegal.

bands.name: ISM 433 MHz Band
likely_sources: Car key fobs / remote locking (433.92 MHz)
bands.notes: Very common band for cheap wireless devices. Numerous short bursts normal.

bands.name: GSM-900 Uplink (880–915 MHz)
likely_sources: Mobile phone uplink (Orange, SFR, Bouygues, Free)
bands.notes: Uplink from handset to tower. Close-range phones will be strongest.

bands.name: GSM-900 / 4G-900 Downlink (925–960 MHz)
likely_sources: Mobile network base stations (Orange, SFR, Bouygues, Free)

bands.name: ISM 868 MHz (EU LoRa / SigFox / Smart Meters)
likely_sources: Enedis Linky smart meter (Wavenis 868 MHz module)
bands.notes: Linky meters use Wavenis at 868 MHz in some areas; newer rollouts may use Wize at 169 MHz or PLC.

bands.name: Enedis Linky / Wize Smart Meters (169 MHz)
likely_sources: Enedis Linky smart meter (Wize protocol at 169.4–169.6 MHz)
bands.notes: Some Linky deployments use the Wize / Wavenis-ULP protocol at 169 MHz (200 Hz channels).

bands.name: DVB-T2 / TNT Digital Television (470–790 MHz)
likely_sources: TNT multiplexes R1–R8 (TF1, France 2, France 3, Canal+, France 5, M6, Arte, etc.)
bands.notes: French terrestrial digital TV (TNT) uses DVB-T2, 8 MHz channels in UHF band IV/V. Signal should be ~8 MHz wide. The HackRF can receive but not decode directly without a DVB-T software stack.

bands.name: 4G LTE Band 20 Downlink — 800 MHz (791–821 MHz)
likely_sources: 4G LTE base stations (Orange, SFR, Bouygues, Free — Band 20)
Rural area coverage — Band 20 is the primary rural 4G band in France
bands.notes: LTE Band 20 (800 MHz) is the backbone of French rural 4G coverage. Very widely deployed. Each operator has ~10 MHz of spectrum here.

bands.name: 4G LTE Band 20 Uplink — 800 MHz (832–862 MHz)
likely_sources: Mobile phone uplink to base station (Orange, SFR, Bouygues, Free — Band 20)
bands.notes: Uplink pair for LTE Band 20. 41 MHz duplex gap from the downlink at 791–821 MHz.

bands.name: GSM-R Railway Communications (876–925 MHz)
likely_sources: SNCF locomotive to control centre voice / data
bands.notes: GSM-R uses 876–880 MHz uplink and 921–925 MHz downlink in France. Audible only near railway lines. Being phased out for FRMCS (5G) from ~2030.

bands.name: ADS-B Mode S (1090 MHz)
likely_sources: Aircraft ADS-B transponders (position, altitude, ICAO ID)

bands.name: GPS L1 (1575.42 MHz)
likely_sources: GPS satellites (BPSK spread-spectrum — normally below noise floor)
bands.notes: GPS is normally below the noise floor of an SDR without a dedicated LNA. A visible signal here may indicate a GPS jammer or repeater.

bands.name: Amateur 23cm Band (1240–1300 MHz)
bands.notes: Shared with radiolocation (radar). Secondary allocation for amateurs in France. Rarely active except near club stations.

bands.name: GSM-1800 / 4G-1800 Uplink (1710–1785 MHz)
likely_sources: Mobile phone uplink (Orange, SFR, Bouygues, Free — 2G/4G)

bands.name: GSM-1800 / 4G-1800 Downlink (1805–1880 MHz)
likely_sources: Mobile network base stations (2G/4G LTE Band 3)

bands.name: DECT Cordless Phones (1880–1900 MHz)
bands.notes: Normal in residential areas but can cause interference to other devices. DECT uses TDMA — you may see brief bursts.

bands.name: 3G UMTS (1920–2170 MHz)
likely_sources: 3G UMTS mobile network (being phased out in France)

bands.name: HDMI / DisplayPort Cable Radiation
likely_sources: HDMI cable acting as antenna for pixel clock harmonics
USB 3.x cable (5 Gbps = harmonics at 625 MHz, 1.25 GHz)
bands.notes: HDMI radiates strongly at pixel clock harmonics (typically 74.25 MHz * N). This is one of the most common RFI sources in modern homes. Try disconnecting HDMI cables to identify.

bands.name: Switching PSU Harmonics (UHF range)
likely_sources: LED driver / LED strip power supply
bands.notes: Switching harmonics can extend well into UHF. Cheap chargers and LED power supplies are particularly bad. Look for regularly-spaced spectral lines.

bands.name: ISM 2.4 GHz — Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / Zigbee (2400–2484 MHz)
likely_sources: Microwave oven leakage (~2.45 GHz, broadband bursts during cooking)
bands.notes: Extremely busy band in residential areas. Microwave ovens cause broadband bursts at ~2.45 GHz when running — easily identified by the cooking cycle. Wi-Fi channels 1, 6, and 11 are non-overlapping in France. HackRF sensitivity drops above ~2 GHz; use a dedicated LNA for reliable reception here.

bands.name: 4G LTE Band 7 — 2600 MHz (2500–2690 MHz)
bands.notes: At the upper edge of HackRF range — sensitivity is reduced.

bands.name: 5G NR Band n78 — 3.5 GHz (3400–3800 MHz)
likely_sources: 5G NR base stations (Orange, SFR, Bouygues, Free — all four operators)
bands.notes: The primary French 5G band. All four operators hold spectrum here following the 2020 auction. HackRF can receive this band but sensitivity is low above 2.5 GHz; an external LNA is strongly recommended. Each operator has 80–100 MHz of bandwidth.
